newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Nanyang economists see Singapore 97 GDP at 6.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Nanyang economists see Singapore 97 GDP at 6.5 pct.

text.p: The Econometric Modelling Unit of Nanyang Technological University on Thursday predicted Singapore real gross domestic product at 6.5 percent in 1997 with a surge to 8.8 percent in 1988.
The revised forecast for this year compares with one of 7.2 percent made in January although there are signs of recovery, said Chen Kang, head of the Econometric Modelling Unit.
"Available evidence does confirm that the electronics industry is already in the process of recovery," he said.
He was speaking in Singapore at The Third International Conference on Forecasting the Singapore Economy and Annual Review of Central Banking Polices in Asia.
He said trade data so far this year had yet to confirm a clear trend of recovery for the manufacturing sector and other signals to date were conflicting.

While market indicators looked positive and investment commitments had been strong in the first quarter, non-oil domestic exports to the United States and Japan had remained weak in the past three months, even though there had been some signs of a pickup in global electronics demand.
External demand for personal computers shows no signs of picking up and disk drives, Singapore's major export product, face softer prices and serious stock adjustments, Chen said.

The Econometric Modelling Unit forecast that in 1997 the manufacturing sector will grow at 4.9 percent, up from 3.4 perent in 1996, with the construction sector expected to post double digit growth of 10.6 percent although this is well down on the 1996 figure of 18.4 percent.
The other three major sectors of commerce, transport and communication and financial and business services are seen performing better than last year at 7.6, 8.7 and 8.6 percent respectively.
Non-oil export growth is seen running at seven percent this year, little changed from last year as the recovery in demand for electronic goods remains less than robust.

Chen said the major export markets of the U.S. and Malaysia remained difficult although domestic exports of integrated circuits, computer parts and peripherals to Malaysia can be expected to have a healthy recovery.
In the U.S., strong growth in portable computers and adaptor units are expected but they will not be able to make up the shortfall in other major export products, he said.
"Projecting into the longer-term future, Singapore's manufacturing industry is increasingly facing new and fierce competition from emerging economies," Chen said.

"As Singapore moves further up the growth ladder it becomes harder to create comparative advantage and be innovative. Efforts by the government to promote the chemical and petroleum industries must be seen as welcome steps."
